intro: Mengelberg’s Concertgebouw recording combines a compact overall span with flexible phrasing and coordinated string slides. The supplied transfer joins the two sides of Columbia L 1798; its 7:17 duration is a property of this transfer, not a metronome marking.
question: How can a seven-minute Adagietto leave room for both forward motion and broadening?

cues.title: Strings and harp alone
cues.text: The Adagietto removes winds, brass and percussion from the Fifth Symphony’s orchestra. In this recording, concentrate on how the strings connect notes above the harp rather than expecting changes of instrumental family.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s Adagietto score specifies strings and harp; the original Columbia L 1798 label identifies Mengelberg and the Concertgebouw Orchestra. This is a whole-movement observation, not an isolated entrance.

cues.title: Sliding together
cues.text: Listen across the string phrases for portamento: an audible slide between pitches. Yale’s account of this particular recording describes the slides as coordinated within the sections, rather than independent expressive gestures by individual players.
cues.evidence: Yale University Library, Studying Performance Practice Through Sound Recordings, Gustav Mahler, Mengelberg: A Closer Look: https://guides.library.yale.edu/c.php?g=525668&p=4452898. The observation concerns the performance generally; no slide is pinpointed at 0:45.

cues.title: Forward without rigidity
cues.text: A short overall duration does not mean an unchanging beat. Yale describes forward-moving pickups, gradual changes of pulse and sudden stretches in Mengelberg’s phrasing; follow the shape of a phrase rather than imposing one speed on it.
cues.evidence: Yale’s Mengelberg discussion specifically describes the 1926 Adagietto’s pickups, rubato and ritardandi. This cue makes no timestamped claim about a particular pickup.

cues.title: A disc in circulation
cues.text: A New Zealand newspaper reviewed Columbia L 1798 in March 1928, naming Mengelberg and the Concertgebouw Orchestra. The notice establishes that this performance was already circulating as a record, independently of its recording-session date.
cues.evidence: Wanganui Chronicle, 3 March 1928, p. 18, Recorded Music, Columbia Notes, A Little-known Composer: https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/WC19280303.2.96.16.2.

cues.title: Two sides already joined
cues.text: The original issue occupied both sides of Columbia L 1798. This source supplies them in one file; neither the join nor the transfer’s playback speed should be mistaken for an instruction by Mahler.
cues.evidence: Internet Archive lists matrices (W)AX 1548 and 1549 and supplies one 437.23-second FLAC with an MP3 derivative. The label specifies Speed 80, while the uploader describes a 78-rpm transfer; actual playback-speed calibration and splice location are not established.

cues.title: A more patient return
cues.text: In the returning opening material, compare the phrase’s breadth with its first appearance. Yale singles out Mengelberg’s slower beginning of the returning theme; that local broadening coexists with the performance’s short total duration.
cues.evidence: Yale describes the slower returning theme. cache/analysis/mahler-5-adagietto-mengelberg-1926.txt records a boundary at 4:46 and a level dip around 4:50; the provisional comparison map places the Peabody return region near 4:48 here. This is passage-level, not bar-aligned.

cues.title: The later crest
cues.text: The final large swell sustains its pressure rather than passing through one isolated accent. Follow the long crest and compare its duration with the quieter stretches that precede it.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/mahler-5-adagietto-mengelberg-1926.txt: five-second relative-level windows remain near −9 to −10 dB from 6:20 to 6:50, including the loudest window at 6:35. These are within-file levels, not orchestral dynamic markings.

cues.title: Decay and transfer noise
cues.text: The ending withdraws into the residual sound of the transfer. Distinguish the diminishing musical resonance from the surface noise: the file continues after its sustained crest has fallen away.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/mahler-5-adagietto-mengelberg-1926.txt: boundary at 6:58; relative level falls from −11.8 dB at 6:55 to −26.5 at 7:05 and −44.4 at 7:15. Total decoded duration is 437.2 seconds; no exact final-note release is asserted.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
